rationale: The book's core identification — a sign is a message given ahead of events (an oracle, a scene, or a prophet's lived story) whose truth is proven by fulfillment, as opposed to a wonder conjured on demand — is carried better by the cited texts than the common 'authenticating miracle' reading. Isaiah 7:14 is decisive on its own terms: on the day the sign was given nothing miraculous occurred in Ahaz's court; the word itself stood as the sign for centuries, and the miracle belongs to the fulfillment. Ezekiel 24:24 explicitly makes the man and his acted story the sign, verified 'when this cometh.' Luke 11:30 defines Jonah as the sign given precisely in refusal of a demanded wonder. The book further explains data the common reading must shunt into a 'minority' category: the 1 Samuel 10 signs to Saul are entirely non-miraculous foretold scenes (travelers, loaves, a greeting), and Luke 2:12's sign to the shepherds is simply a scene announced in advance. The Deuteronomy 18:21-22 test ('if the thing follow not, nor come to pass') presupposes that a sign is by nature a predicted thing awaiting fulfillment — a criterion unintelligible if a sign is essentially an on-the-spot wonder. The strongest counter (sign = perceptible act, characteristically a miracle, that authenticates God's messenger, per John 2:11; 20:30-31; Exodus 4; Acts 2:22) is largely a broader functional label rather than a contradicting core: the book does not deny that fulfillments may be miraculous or that signs authenticate; it relocates the sign to the advance word and its verification. However, the counter does press real scope objections — Johannine miracle-signs performed publicly without a prior spoken prediction, Exodus 4's on-the-spot wonders called signs, and the perpetual covenant signs (rainbow, circumcision, sabbath) that point to a standing covenant rather than forward — which the book's chapter absorbs (it explicitly concedes a 'second family' of covenant signs) but the printed entry does not. So the core is established while the entry's implicit universality remains disputed: CORE_ONLY.
book_core_identification: A 'sign' is a message given in advance of events — an oracle, a foretold scene, or a prophet's own lived story — whose fulfillment testifies to its divine origin; it is contrasted with a wonder performed on demand.
book_secondary_elaborations: The entry's implicit claim of exhaustiveness — that this predictive-fulfillment sense covers biblical 'sign' usage generally (the chapter itself concedes a second family of covenant signs: rainbow, circumcision, Passover blood, sabbath)
The two Mosaic validity tests (Deut 18:21-22 fulfillment; Deut 13:1-3 fidelity to the law overriding fulfillment)
The extension into 'similitudes' — whole lives (Hosea, Abraham/Isaac, Joseph, Rahab, Israel) as composed lived prophecies, warranted by Ecclesiastes 1:9; 3:15 and Paul's typos method
The claim that history itself is composed and repeatable ('God requireth that which is past')
strongest_counter_interpretation: The mainstream reading (Response A primary, shared by B and C): a sign is a visible act, event, or object — most characteristically a miraculous work — that points beyond itself to God's presence and authenticates His messenger, with the Johannine miracle-signs (John 2:11; 20:30-31), the Exodus wonders (Exod 4:1-9; 7:3), and Acts 2:22 as the paradigm; predictive and prophetic-sign-act uses are treated as sub-categories of this broader pointer/authenticator function.
counter_core_identification: A sign is a perceptible pointer — paradigmatically a miracle — that discloses divine identity and authenticates God's messenger, calling observers to faith.
material_core_denial: The counter would have to deny that the essence of a biblical sign lies in the advance-given word or enacted life verified by fulfillment, insisting instead that the sign is the wondrous event itself at the moment of performance. But the counter as actually formulated does not deny fulfillment-testimony; it subsumes it, making it a broader label rather than an incompatible referent.
counter_case: John 2:11 and 20:30-31 call Jesus' publicly performed miracles 'signs' with no prior spoken prediction attached to each act — the miracle itself functions as the sign
Exodus 4:1-9 presents on-the-spot wonders (rod, leprous hand, water to blood) explicitly given 'that they may believe' — authentication by wonder
Acts 2:22 and Hebrews 2:3-4 describe God attesting Jesus and the apostles 'by signs and wonders,' pairing the terms as near-synonyms of miraculous attestation
The covenant signs (Gen 9:12-17; 17:11; Exod 31:13-17) point to a standing relationship, not forward to a fulfillment, resisting the 'prophecy given in advance' definition
Nicodemus's inference in John 3:2 ('no man can do these signs except God be with him') treats sign-working as immediate divine authentication
book_explanatory_advantages: Isaiah 7:14: no wonder occurred when the sign was given; the word stood as the sign for centuries before its miraculous fulfillment — the book's distinction between sign (advance message) and miracle (fulfillment) fits the text exactly

Ezekiel 24:24 and Isaiah 8:18; 20:3: the prophet himself, his acted story, is the sign, verified 'when this cometh' — evidence the miracle-paradigm must file under a separate 'prophetic sign-act' category while the book unifies it
Luke 11:29-30 / Mark 8:11-12: the demanded wonder is refused and the sign of Jonah given instead — the gospels themselves draw the book's exact contrast between sign given and wonder demanded

1 Samuel 10:2-9: entirely non-miraculous foretold scenes are called 'signs,' and 'all those signs came to pass that day' — inexplicable as authenticating miracles, natural as advance-given words fulfilled
Luke 2:12: the shepherds' sign is simply a scene announced ahead of finding it
Deuteronomy 18:21-22 defines sign-validity by whether 'the thing follow... or come to pass,' presupposing signs are predictive by nature; Deut 13:1-3 speaks of a sign that 'come to pass'

The definition scales coherently into the NT typology the chapter documents (Hos 11:1/Matt 2:15; Heb 11:19 'en parabolē'; 1 Pet 3:21 'antitypon'), where lives and histories function as signs fulfilled in Christ
counter_explanatory_advantages: Directly explains Johannine miracle-signs performed without an attached prior prediction (John 2:11)
Directly explains Exodus 4's on-the-spot wonders called signs, given for immediate authentication
Naturally accommodates 'signs and wonders' word-pairing (Acts 2:22; Heb 2:4) as overlapping miracle vocabulary
Accommodates covenant signs as pointers without needing a forward-looking fulfillment
decisive_sources: Isaiah 7:14 (sign given with no wonder performed at the giving; fulfillment centuries later)
Ezekiel 24:24 (the prophet's acted life is the sign, known 'when this cometh')
Luke 11:29-30 with Mark 8:11-12 (wonder-on-demand refused; Jonah given as the sign)
1 Samuel 10:2-9 (non-miraculous foretold scenes called signs, 'all those signs came to pass that day')
Luke 2:12 (a scene told in advance as the sign)
Deuteronomy 18:21-22 and 13:1-3 (sign-validity defined by coming to pass)
Isaiah 8:18; 20:3; Hosea 1-3 (prophets and their lives as signs)
unresolved_objections: The Johannine miracle-signs (John 2:11; 6:2; 20:30-31) are wondrous acts called signs without a prior spoken prediction for each; the book explains them as 'lived signs' fulfilling OT patterns, which requires an extra interpretive step the counter does not need

The covenant signs (Gen 9; 17; Exod 31) point to a standing covenant rather than forward to fulfillment; the book's chapter concedes this as a 'second family,' meaning the printed entry's definition is not exhaustive of biblical usage

Exodus 4:1-9's signs before Israel are wonders performed to produce belief, fitting the authentication paradigm more directly than the advance-word paradigm (though they were foretold to Moses and not demanded by him)
The broader 'similitude' program (all histories as composed prophecies, Eccl 1:9 read via a symbolic sun) is a secondary elaboration not established by the sign evidence itself
